1107.title: Who doesn't fast
1107.hook: the ill, travelers, pregnant and nursing women, the elderly, and menstruating women
1107.howItsDone: Muslims who are ill, traveling, pregnant, nursing or elderly may leave the Ramadan fast, and women do not fast during menstruation or after childbirth; the days are made up later by those who can, and those who never can feed a poor person instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what breaks the fast: eating, drinking and intimacy on purpose. The one who forgot simply finishes the day; forgetting is Allah's gift.

Travelers on the road in Ramadan with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Some are fasting. Some are eating. They ride together, stop together, and, the report says, nobody blames anybody: the fasting don't look down on the eating, and the eating don't look down on the fasting. It's a small scene, told by his companion Anas, and it shows a softer side of the pillar. The fast has an exit door built into the very verses that command it.
screen: `TRAVELERS ON THE ROAD IN RAMADAN.` → `SOME FAST, SOME EAT.` → `NOBODY BLAMES ANYBODY.`

segments.voice: The word is rukhsah: a concession, an allowance Allah has made. First, it sits right next to the command. Surah two, in Pickthall's words: "and (for) him who is sick among you, or on a journey, (the same) number of other days." The sick and the traveler may leave the fast and keep it another time. The next verse says why: "Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you." Second, the list grows. A report in the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others says Allah has lifted the fast from the traveler, and from the pregnant and the nursing woman. Scholars also excuse someone too old or frail to fast at all; a later day comes back to what they do instead. And a woman during her period does not fast; the legal books treat the bleeding after childbirth the same way. Aisha, the Prophet's wife, said in a report in Sahih Muslim that they were told to make up missed fasts but not missed prayers. For her it isn't a concession to choose; it's a time the fast doesn't apply. Third, taking the allowance is not a lesser path. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad has the Prophet ﷺ say that Allah loves for his concessions to be taken. Scholars discuss when a traveler should fast and when an illness is serious enough, but the principle is plain: hardship that harms is not what the fast is for. Fourth, Anas's road. Nobody judges. For anyone keeping a practice next to someone who, today, isn't: the reasons may be invisible, and in this teaching, they're between that person and Allah.

segments.voice: Run slowly through the list, the sick, the traveler, the pregnant, the nursing, the elderly, the woman in her period, and let a face come to mind for one of them. Then turn to yourself: is there a rule you keep, about work, food, exercise, anything, even when it hurts you? Just notice it, and if you pray, ask Allah for ease.
Rukhsah. A concession: the permission not to fast when illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, age or a woman's period make it a hardship. Today's word.
Your line: the fast bends. Ease is part of the command. Until tomorrow.

1108.title: Making it up
1108.hook: missed days are made up later, or a poor person fed for each day if unable
1108.howItsDone: Muslims who miss Ramadan fasts for illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing or menstruation fast the same number of days later in the year, before the next Ramadan, together or spread out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rukhsah, the allowance: the fast bends for the sick, the traveler, the pregnant and the nursing, and more.

It's Sha'ban, the month before Ramadan, and in a house in Medina a woman is keeping fasts that belong to last Ramadan. She isn't adding anything extra. She's paying back. The woman is Aisha, wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she says it herself in Sahih al-Bukhari: she would have days of Ramadan to make up, and she couldn't make them up until Sha'ban. Months could pass with that small debt waiting. Today's word is the name for paying it.
screen: `THE MONTH BEFORE RAMADAN.` → `AISHA, KEEPING OLD FASTS.` → `PAYING BACK.`

segments.voice: The word is qada': making up an act of worship after its time has passed. First, it comes straight from yesterday's verse. The sick and the traveler fast, in Pickthall's words, "(the same) number of other days." The next verse gives a reason: Allah desires ease, and desires "that ye should complete the period." So the allowance doesn't erase the days. It moves them. Second, Aisha shows the timing can be loose. She made up her days in Sha'ban, just before the next Ramadan. Scholars take from this that make-up days can wait, though not past the next Ramadan; schools differ on what's owed if someone lets them slide past that without a reason. Third, the days don't have to be in a row. The verse says only other days, and scholars read that as allowing them to be spread out: a Monday here, a Thursday there, a quiet Saturday in winter when the days are short. Yesterday's report from Aisha in Sahih Muslim fits here too: women make up the fasts missed during their periods. Fourth, one more case, and tomorrow is about it. Some people will never be able to make the days up: the very old, the permanently ill. For them the verse has another answer, and it involves feeding someone. Away from the fast, qada' is a way of thinking about any commitment you couldn't keep on time. Not canceled. Not a failure. Owed, and waiting for its day.

segments.voice: If you fast and owe days, see a calendar in your mind and quietly place them, which weeks, which days, before the next Ramadan. If you don't, find one thing you meant to do and didn't, a call you owe, a thank-you note, a visit you postponed, and without scolding yourself, give it a date. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make it easy.
Qada'. Making up a missed act of worship after its time; here, fasting the missed days of Ramadan later in the year. Today's word.
Your line: made up later. The days are moved, never simply erased. See you tomorrow.

1109.title: Feeding instead
1109.hook: those who can never fast feed a poor person each day
1109.howItsDone: Muslims who are too old or chronically ill ever to fast pay fidyah, feeding a poor person for each missed day of Ramadan, sometimes through a mosque or charity that sets a figure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qada': made up later. Missed fasts aren't erased, only moved, and Aisha paid hers back in Sha'ban.

A grandmother sits at the iftar table every evening of Ramadan. She hasn't fasted in years. Her body can't do it anymore, and her doctor has said so plainly. Yesterday's answer, make the days up later, doesn't help her: there is no later when she'll be stronger. So is she outside the fast now, watching from the edge of the table? The verse that gave the sick and the traveler their other days has one more line. It gives her a way to take part.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER AT THE IFTAR TABLE.` → `NO LATER WHEN SHE'LL BE STRONGER.` → `ONE MORE LINE IN THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: The word is fidyah. First, the verse. Surah two, verse one hundred eighty-four, after the sick and the traveler, says in Pickthall's words that there is "a ransom: the feeding of a man in need." Fidyah is something given in place of something else: here, a meal for a person in need, in place of a day of fasting. Second, who it's for. Readers have argued over this verse, because it can sound as though anyone may feed instead of fasting. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari gives the reading of Ibn Abbas, the Prophet's cousin: the verse is for the old man and the old woman who cannot fast; they feed a poor person for each day. Scholars extend that to people with a lasting illness and no hope of recovery. So fidyah is for those for whom qada' will never be possible. Third, how it's done. The schools differ on the measure, a portion of grain or its value, or a meal, and on whether it's paid day by day or all at once. Some mosques and charities publish a figure each Ramadan, and some families pay it on behalf of a parent. The same verse adds that whoever does more good of their own accord, it is better for them. Fourth, why this matters. The fast isn't only about the person who's hungry; it turns toward the one who is hungry every day. When a body can no longer fast, the fast doesn't disappear. It becomes a plate set in front of someone else.
screen: `FIDYAH: GIVEN IN PLACE OF.` · `FOR THOSE WHO CAN NEVER FAST.` · `ONE PERSON FED FOR EACH DAY.` · `THE FAST BECOMES A PLATE.` · then, large: `A RANSOM: THE FEEDING OF A MAN IN NEED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who can no longer do something they once loved, an older relative, a friend who's ill, a neighbor who doesn't leave the house. Then plan one meal, or the cost of one, to give to someone hungry, quietly, with that person in your heart. If they owe fidyah, you might offer to help them pay it, and if you pray, remember them in it.
Fidyah. Feeding a person in need for each day of Ramadan, given by those who can never fast or make the days up. Today's word.
Your line: feed instead. When you can't give what was asked, you give what you still can. Same time tomorrow.

1110.title: The soul of the fast
1110.hook: the fast is a shield, so don't shout or quarrel (Bukhari)
1110.howItsDone: Muslims who are fasting try to guard their speech and temper as well as their stomachs, and when provoked some say, as the Prophet taught, "I am fasting."

segments.voice: Yesterday, fidyah: feed instead. Those who can never fast feed a person in need for each day.

Five in the evening, the last hour of a long fasting day. Blood sugar is low, traffic is worse, and someone cuts in line at the store. Every part of the body wants to say something sharp. The past days were about the rules: the intention, what breaks the fast, who's excused, how days are made up. All of it about the stomach. But the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said something about the fast that has nothing to do with food, and everything to do with that moment in the line.
screen: `THE LAST HOUR, A LONG LINE.` → `THE RULES WERE ABOUT FOOD.` → `THIS IS ABOUT THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: First, the image. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet ﷺ says the fast is a junnah, a shield, held up between you and what would hurt you. In the same report he says what it's for: when one of you is fasting, don't speak obscenely and don't shout. And if someone insults you or picks a fight, say: I am fasting. Not a comeback. A reminder, as much to yourself as to them. Second, without this, the fast can go hollow. Another report in Bukhari is blunt: whoever doesn't give up lying and acting on lies, Allah has no need of them giving up their food and drink. An empty stomach and a sharp tongue, in this report, don't add up to a fast. Third, it connects to the purpose surah two gave on the first day of this part: the fast is prescribed so that, in Pickthall's words, "ye may ward off (evil)." The shield and the warding off are close pictures. In this reading, hunger is the training, and what's guarded is what comes out of a person when they're tired and provoked. Fourth, the same report carries a saying from Allah, a hadith qudsi: every deed of a person is for them, except fasting, which is for Allah, and Allah rewards it. Some teachers say that's because no one else can see a fast: a secret between a person and Allah, whose proof shows in how they treat the person in front of them. Fasting or not, the shield works the same way: one sentence, said quietly, before the sharp one.
screen: `JUNNAH: THE FAST IS A SHIELD.` · `SAY: I AM FASTING.` · `NO LIES, OR THE FAST IS HOLLOW.` · `A SECRET BETWEEN A PERSON AND ALLAH.` · then, large: `THAT YE MAY WARD OFF (EVIL).`

segments.voice: Picture where your temper is most likely to slip today, a meeting, a commute, a sibling, a comment section, and see it coming. Choose your shield sentence: if you're fasting, it can be the Prophet's, I am fasting; if not, any short line that reminds you who you mean to be. Say it silently on each out-breath until it feels ready, and if you pray, ask Allah for patience.
The soul of the fast. The fast as a shield: no shouting, no quarreling, no lies; and when provoked, I am fasting. Today's word.

1111.title: Mondays and Thursdays
1111.hook: the Prophet ﷺ fasted Mondays and Thursdays (Tirmidhi)
1111.howItsDone: Some Muslims keep voluntary fasts on Mondays and Thursdays through the year, following the Prophet's practice, eating before dawn and breaking the fast at sunset as in Ramadan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soul of the fast: a shield. No shouting, no quarrels, and when provoked, I am fasting.

Ramadan comes once a year. But in some Muslim homes there's a quieter rhythm: an alarm set before dawn on a Sunday night, a glass of water and some dates, and then a regular Monday at work, fasting, without anyone at the next desk knowing. Then the same again on Wednesday night, for Thursday. No holiday. No crowd at iftar. Just a habit with roots in the week of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
screen: `AN ALARM ON A SUNDAY NIGHT.` → `A REGULAR MONDAY, FASTING.` → `NO CROWD, NO HOLIDAY.`

segments.voice: First, the practice itself. Reports in the collections describe the Prophet ﷺ making a point of fasting on Mondays and Thursdays. These are voluntary fasts, sunnah, not required. Much of what shapes the Ramadan fast still shapes them: dawn to sunset, food, drink and intimacy set aside, the shield on the tongue. But nobody owes them. Second, why those two days. In a report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, the Prophet ﷺ says deeds are presented on Monday and Thursday, and he loved that his deeds be presented while he was fasting: an accounting, twice a week, and wanting to be found in the middle of a good act when it comes. Third, Monday has its own reason. In Sahih Muslim he is asked about fasting on Monday, and he answers: that is the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me. So the Monday fast is also a kind of remembering, a small anniversary kept every week. Fourth, the rhythm. A yearly fast is a mountain; a weekly one is a path you walk often. Some teachers describe voluntary fasts as a way to keep what Ramadan builds from fading over the year. And yesterday's shield goes with it: a regular Monday where the tongue is guarded and nobody else even knows. Big seasons matter. A weekly fast is something else: small, chosen, and repeated.
screen: `A VOLUNTARY FAST, TWICE A WEEK.` · `DEEDS PRESENTED, WHILE FASTING.` · `MONDAY: BORN, AND REVELATION.` · `A PATH, NOT A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Look ahead to the next Monday or Thursday. If you fast, and it's safe for your health, see yourself setting the alarm the night before, eating before dawn, and going through that ordinary day fasting. If you don't, choose one small thing to set aside that day from dawn to sunset as a way of marking it, a snack, your phone at lunch, a complaint, and if you pray, make it an intention.
Mondays and Thursdays. The voluntary weekly fasts the Prophet ﷺ kept: the days deeds are presented, and Monday, the day of his birth and of revelation. Today's word.
Your line: two days a week. Monday also remembers a birth and a revelation. Rest well.

1112.title: The white days
1112.hook: three days in the middle of each lunar month
1112.howItsDone: Some Muslims fast the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of each lunar month, checking a lunar calendar or their mosque's notices to know when those days fall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mondays and Thursdays: two days a week, a voluntary fast on the days deeds are presented.

On the right night of the month, the street is lit without a single lamp. The moon is full, or close to it, and the whole sky is pale. Islam keeps its calendar by that same moon: each month begins with a thin crescent, swells to a round white face in the middle, and thins away again. And right there, at the bright middle of every month, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ pointed his companions to three days of fasting. Not a month, like Ramadan. Not two days every week. Three days, when the nights are at their brightest.
screen: `A STREET LIT BY THE MOON.` → `A CALENDAR KEPT BY THE MOON.` → `THREE DAYS AT THE BRIGHT MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, the habit itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Abu Hurayrah says his close friend, meaning the Prophet, advised him to keep three things: fasting three days of every month, two units of prayer in the morning, and the witr prayer before sleep. A small, steady thing, handed to one person as friendly advice. Second, which three. A report in the collection of al-Tirmidhi has the Prophet telling Abu Dharr that if he fasts three days of a month, let it be the thirteenth, the fourteenth and the fifteenth: the middle days of a lunar month, around the full moon. Tradition calls them the white days, and tradition says the name comes from the nights, white with moonlight from dusk to dawn. Third, why three. Another hadith in Bukhari, from the conversation with Abdullah ibn Amr that we'll meet tomorrow, says each good deed is counted ten times over, so fasting three days a month is like fasting all the time. The point isn't arithmetic: something small and regular is treated as something large. Fourth, how people keep it. Because the dates follow the moon, the white days move against the calendar on the wall. Some Muslims check a lunar calendar each month, or an app, or the mosque's notice board, and mark the thirteenth to the fifteenth. Some fast all three, some one or two. It's voluntary, and nobody is blamed for missing it. The white days are simply there, every month, for anyone who wants them.
screen: `ADVICE FROM A FRIEND: THREE DAYS A MONTH.` · `THE THIRTEENTH, FOURTEENTH, FIFTEENTH.` · `SMALL AND REGULAR, COUNTED LARGE.` · `THE DATES MOVE WITH THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Picture the moon as you last saw it: thin, half, or round? You don't need the date; just ask where you'll be when it's round next, at work, at home, traveling. If you're Muslim and you fast, you might choose one of those three days to try; if not, one of those nights simply to step outside and look up.
The white days. The thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of each lunar month, around the full moon, kept by some Muslims as three voluntary fasts. Today's word.
Your line: the full-moon days. Three days at the bright middle of every month. Tomorrow: the fast of Dawud.

1113.title: The fast of Dawud
1113.hook: a day on, a day off, the most beloved fast (Bukhari)
1113.carry: a day on, a day off
1113.howItsDone: Some Muslims keep the fast of Dawud, fasting every other day, and the story of Abdullah ibn Amr is told as a caution against taking on more than one can sustain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the white days: the full-moon days, three voluntary fasts at the bright middle of each month.

What do you do with someone who wants to do too much good? Abdullah ibn Amr was a companion with a big plan. Word reached the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that Abdullah had vowed to fast every single day and stand in prayer every single night, for as long as he lived. The Prophet came to him and asked if it was true. It was. What came next wasn't praise, and it wasn't a scolding either. It was a negotiation, step by step, that ended at a fast with a name.
screen: `TOO MUCH GOOD?` → `EVERY DAY, EVERY NIGHT.` → `A NEGOTIATION.`

segments.voice: First, the bargaining, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet tells Abdullah: you can't keep that up. Fast and break your fast, sleep and stand in prayer. Fast three days a month. Abdullah says he can do more. More is offered, and he asks for more again, until the Prophet says: then fast the fast of Dawud. Fast a day, and break a day. When Abdullah asks for still more, the answer is that there is nothing better than that. Second, the reason. In the same report the Prophet tells him his body has a right over him, and his eyes, and his wife, and his guests. Worship isn't meant to swallow the rest of a life. Third, the name. Dawud is David, the prophet the Qur'an remembers for the psalms he was given. Another hadith in Bukhari says the most beloved fast to Allah is the fast of Dawud, who fasted one day and not the next, and the most beloved prayer is his: sleeping, rising, and sleeping again. A rhythm, not a marathon. Fourth, the ending. Abdullah lives long, and in old age he wishes he had taken the Prophet's easier offer. Another version in Bukhari says he kept to his word anyway: a companion, preserved in the collection, admitting he asked for too much. The same thread runs through this week: the fast bends, missed days are made up, some feed instead, the fast is a shield, two days a week, three days a month. And today, at the far edge of what's encouraged, a day on and a day off, with rest built in.
screen: `ABDULLAH ASKS FOR MORE.` · `YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.` · `DAWUD'S RHYTHM: ON, THEN OFF.` · `AN OLD MAN KEEPS HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Breathe in and out slowly, and notice the rhythm: effort, then rest; neither is better than the other, and the breath needs both. Then think of one thing you've been doing every single day without a break, and ask what a day off from it would look like. Don't decide anything; just let the question breathe with you.
The fast of Dawud. Fasting one day and eating the next, named for the prophet David, and called in Bukhari the most beloved fast to Allah. Today's word.
Your line: a day on, a day off. Rest is part of the rhythm. Another week, done.
